subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a short statement on the ordering of our business based on a statement made in the house last evening by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas). I should like to quote what he said as found on page 6303 of Hansard:
I am suggesting two things: first, that the government be prepared to postpone the flag issue, after the amendment has been voted on, until the fall.
That is the amendment now before the house. He continued:
I am suggesting that when we come to the flag debate we vote on the amendment which was moved by the official opposition, and then adjourn the debate until we meet some time in the fall.
He then continued and said:
-if the government will agree to that, I suggest that the opposition groups agree to an order of the house which would limit the debate on the flag, when it comes up, to a period of one week.
The hon. member then went on to say:
There would be no value at all in postponing the flag debate unless when it does come up the time is limited; for if we are going to spend weeks on the flag debate we would be better to spend that time now, in what would normally be a recess, rather than taking up time this fall which ought to be devoted to some very important legislation,-
The hon. member then said:
1 believe that a compromise could be worked out, if not by the house leaders then by a meeting of the party leaders, in order to get the business of parliament back on the rails, and to see if we cannot dispose quickly of this motion-
That is the motion before the house for interim supply.
-and the legislation dealing with federal-provincial relations, deal with the flag in so far as the amendment is concerned, then adjourn until the fall with an understanding that when we come back we will deal with the flag for only a limited period of time.
Mr. Speaker, I think the suggestions made by the hon. member-and I appreciate the spirit behind these suggestions-are reasonable and deserve the favourable consideration
of this house. I should be glad to discuss with the leaders of the opposition 'parties details regarding how they can immediately be implemented, and for that purpose I will be glad to arrange a meeting later this afternoon.

subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the moment we have before us a motion for interim supply. The Prime Minister did not see fit to deal with this matter in any way. There are 200 questions which have not received any answers from the government, and there has been no endeavour made on the part of the government in any way to meet its constitutional responsibility of giving answers to those questions. We should want to know what the position of the government would be on this matter, which is of prime importance to the proper discharge of the responsibilities of parliament.
As to the suggestions made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, I am sure in this case there was no inspiration in advance for the suggestions made, although there have been a number of instances recently where obvious co-operation has been apparent in questions asked.
However, this is a matter that would require the consideration of the caucus. Our caucus will be meeting tomorrow morning, at which time this question will be discussed and a determination made.

subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext:
Business of the House
concerned about the business of parliament, and we need no suggestions from any other party as to what we think our duty is in trying to make parliament effective.

subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we find the words of the Prime Minister of much interest. I think it is time we in this house began to face up to reality, because I do not think the people of Canada are following with any degree of sympathy what has been going on here these past weeks.
X suggest to the leader of the official opposition that it might be good if he would attend the proposed meeting this afternoon, so he would have something in the end to take back to his caucus tomorrow morning. As far as we are concerned, we will be very pleased to take part in such a meeting this afternoon.

subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we support the proposal made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). In my opinion, it would be a solution to the dilemma now facing parliament.
It is obvious that the Canadian people must be asking themselves what kind of game we are playing and if we could not discuss constructive matters instead of wasting our time as we have been doing for several days.
I feel that if we can find a solution to the problem facing us today, the people and parliament will benefit therefrom.
We are, therefore, willing to attend that meeting, to discuss its outcome in caucus and to take a decision about the proposal which has been made.



On the orders of the day:

subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext: I think this would be the appropriate time to ask the Prime Minister whether he will give the house the assurance that before the conclusion of the debate on interim supply, and I would hope that would be either today or tomorrow, answers could be given to the many questions that have been asked and have remained unanswered throughout the entire debate, the first time in the history of Canadian parliamentary life that a government has sat silent.

subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext: This is the first time in the history of Canadian parliamentary life that such an obvious filibuster has been conducted on interim supply.

subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext: I suggest to the Prime Minister that if he were in better humour he would show a greater desire for the kind of co-operation he requests. I ask him, was it a filibuster in 1962 when for eight days he, as leader of the opposition, led the attack on the government on interim supply for $300 million? Was that a filibuster?

subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext: On that particular point it should be pointed out, as indeed it has been pointed out, that on the occasion to which my hon. friend refers in 1962 there had been no budget, there had been no departmental estimates introduced, and there was no opportunity to discuss the financial policy of the government. This was the only occasion upon which the opposition could discuss supply. The situations are not the same at all. There have been departmental estimates introduced, some of which have been passed already and about which new questions are being asked. The normal course will be followed in connection with this matter.

subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext: I ask the Prime Minister now to definitely give an answer instead of the evasive subtleties in which he has indulged. Does he intend to have the government answer the questions that have been asked? If he says he does not, I am not going to object. It will simply be in keeping with the attitude that has been adopted.

subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext: The answer to this question was given by the Conservative house leader when he said if we would only give up our program they would put through interim supply at once.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege. First I will expose the falsehood of the Prime Minister with regard to the estimates in 1962. There were six departments before the house waiting to be dealt with. The estimates of the Department of Agriculture had been debated in the house, and the Prime Minister himself spoke twice on those estimates. This disposes of his falsehood with regard to the estimates in the fall of 1962.
I made no suggestion that we would dispose of interim supply immediately if they would postpone the flag debate. I asked a question as to what the government had in mind with regard to interim supply and the flag debate and received no answer to that question, just as we have received no answers to the other questions that have been put before the government.

subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, in view of the fact that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre challenged the statement I made as a falsehood, I would like to quote from page 5985 of Hansard for July 24, where the acting house leader was reported as follows:
-on Monday, we will be asking for two months' interim supply.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext: Would the government like to consider three months, if we complete the dominion-provincial fiscal measure and pass interim supply in short order, and then adjourn?

subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext: Isn't that what he said? A question was asked.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext: On the question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I said I had asked a question of the government and received no answer. The Prime Minister has now disclosed that in fact it was a question. Therefore his earlier statement was false.

subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext: On the same question, Mr. Speaker, I should read the next two sentences.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext: No. We have to conclude the item of business after fiscal arrangements, which is, of course, the flag resolution.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext: I was just being co-operative and I thought the government side would appreciate a holiday.

subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister and it is this. Has the government given consideration, with advice from the special committee on procedure, to how changes could be made in the rules of this house, or how they could be considered by this house, as soon as possible so as to limit the possibility of repetitive, unnecessarily prolonged and obstructive debate in this house?

subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the government is in fact giving consideration to this very important matter, and if a committee of the house is not able to agree on recommendations to the end which my hon. friend has mentioned then we must consider what responsibility the government itself should take in this matter.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext:
I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether it would not be better parliamentary practice for the government to refrain from attempting to impose its will on a committee composed of all members of this house, sitting under Mr. Speaker who is the guardian of the rights and privileges of this house?
Inquiries of the Ministry

subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS TO DISCUSS PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is, of course, no question of the government imposing its will on a committee, but if the committee is not able to make recommendations then the government will have to consider how it can discharge any responsibility it may have in respect of this very important matter.

subtopic: EFFECT OF AUTOMATION ON ECONOMIC AND EMPLOYMENT PROBLEMS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: EFFECT OF AUTOMATION ON ECONOMIC AND EMPLOYMENT PROBLEMS
speechtext:
May I direct a question to the Prime Minister. It is reported that the United States government is going to spend some $2 million on a survey of the effects and impact of automation on the economy and on employment I want to ask the Prime Minister if the Canadian government is giving any thought to a similar study because of growing employment problems that are resulting from increased automation.

Inquiries of the Ministry

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: EFFECT OF AUTOMATION ON ECONOMIC AND EMPLOYMENT PROBLEMS
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, for some time now the Department of Labour has been examining the effects of automation on employment.

subtopic: EFFECT OF AUTOMATION ON ECONOMIC AND EMPLOYMENT PROBLEMS
speechtext:
May I ask a
supplementary question of the Minister of Labour. Will the Minister of Labour consider calling a conference of labour and management so that something could be arrived at as a means of dealing with the effect of automation and technological changes?

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: EFFECT OF AUTOMATION ON ECONOMIC AND EMPLOYMENT PROBLEMS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Department of Labour would be ready to consider such a conference except for the fact that the economic council of Canada has already indicated its intention of holding such a conference this fall, between management and labour.

subtopic: EFFECT OF AUTOMATION ON ECONOMIC AND EMPLOYMENT PROBLEMS
speechtext: As a supplementary question, may I ask the Minister of Labour who is making this study of the impact of automation, and will the report be made public and available to members of the house?

subtopic: EFFECT OF AUTOMATION ON ECONOMIC AND EMPLOYMENT PROBLEMS
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, the economics and research branch of the Department of Labour is involved in considering the impact of automation on employment. The immediate result of these continuing studies is the establishment within the department of a new division called the manpower consultative service, which will engage in dealing with the effects of automation at plant level. That division is a small one because it is new and its members are presently being recruited, but four or five of the top personnel are already at work and it is expected that this division will soon be usefully engaged in activities at plant level.

subtopic: EFFECT OF AUTOMATION ON ECONOMIC AND EMPLOYMENT PROBLEMS
speechtext: As a further supplementary question may I ask the Minister of Labour whether any studies are being made of the broad economic impact of automation, not just at the plant level, and whether such studies will result in a report which could be made available to members of the house.

subtopic: EFFECT OF AUTOMATION ON ECONOMIC AND EMPLOYMENT PROBLEMS
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, I have already mentioned the conference that is proposed for this fall between management and labour. The economics and research branch naturally is involved in this question, and I shall investigate whether any of their studies are suitable for publication and for the general use of hon. members.

subtopic: EFFECT OF AUTOMATION ON ECONOMIC AND EMPLOYMENT PROBLEMS
speechtext:
As a further supplementary question can the minister tell us whether any
[Mr. Douglas.!
meetings have been held with the provinces in order to deal with this automation question, and also whether any agreements have been signed, based on some agreed approach to the problem?

subtopic: EFFECT OF AUTOMATION ON ECONOMIC AND EMPLOYMENT PROBLEMS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as my hon. friend will recall, we did have a meeting of the federal Minister of Labour and the provincial ministers of labour in March of this year, the first such conference held in Canada for many years. One of the items on the agenda was consideration of how the provinces and the federal government might cooperate in this field of automation, particularly in making use of the services of the manpower consultative service.

subtopic: EFFECT OF AUTOMATION ON ECONOMIC AND EMPLOYMENT PROBLEMS
speechtext: One further supplementary, Mr. Speaker. Was any solution arrived at as to what approach should be made as a result of the conference?

subtopic: EFFECT OF AUTOMATION ON ECONOMIC AND EMPLOYMENT PROBLEMS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question is pretty vague and too general to be answered on orders of the day.

subtopic: PROPOSED DISCUSSIONS RESPECTING

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: PROPOSED DISCUSSIONS RESPECTING
subsubtopic: MEETING OF 14 POWER CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs arising out of the answer he gave me yesterday respecting the control commission in Laos. My question is in two parts. Is it the position of the Canadian government that nothing useful can come from trying to arrange for a meeting of the three factions in that country? The other question is was Canada the only member of the control commission which refused to try to arrange a meeting of the three factions?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED DISCUSSIONS RESPECTING
subsubtopic: MEETING OF 14 POWER CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, both questions may be dealt with as one. I think something might flow from an attempt on the part of the three factions to consider the proposal put forward by the foreign minister of the United Kingdom. However Canada, as a member of the control commission, or the commission itself, has, under the Geneva accord, no authority to call a conference. But if the parties themselves are prepared to take action, as I indicated yesterday, we would be only too anxious to give whatever encouragement we could.

subtopic: PROPOSED DISCUSSIONS RESPECTING
subsubtopic: MEETING OF 14 POWER CONFERENCE
speechtext: A supplementary question. The minister has suggested that if the three factions involved showed some disposition to have a meeting, Canada would encourage this. Surely the minister can indicate whether he believes some useful result could come from having a meeting. In other words, if we cannot get the three factions together in order to have a meeting, how will we know whether there is any point in calling a meeting of the much larger group?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED DISCUSSIONS RESPECTING
subsubtopic: MEETING OF 14 POWER CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I neglected to deal with one other aspect of this question, that is the action being taken by Poland and India. This has not yet been communicated to the Canadian member of the commission. I can only say to my hon. friend that under the Geneva accords, both of 1954 and 1962, there is no authority on the part of the commission to do what has been asked. Beyond that it is impossible to go.

subtopic: PROPOSED DISCUSSIONS RESPECTING
subsubtopic: MEETING OF 14 POWER CONFERENCE
speechtext:
A supplementary question to the minister. Since the commission was appointed at the Geneva conference and must report back to the Geneva conference, is there any reason

Inquiries of the Ministry why, if India, Poland and ourselves are agreeable, the commission ought not to report back to the nations that appointed it asking for a further meeting if they find that their task is not being successfully carried out?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED DISCUSSIONS RESPECTING
subsubtopic: MEETING OF 14 POWER CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there would be no reason why a report could not be made by the international control commission, but the Canadian government is of the view that the way to bring peace to Laos at this particular moment is for the parties concerned to live up to the agreements of 1954 and 1962.

subtopic: PROPOSED DISCUSSIONS RESPECTING
subsubtopic: MEETING OF 14 POWER CONFERENCE
speechtext: A supplementary question. In view of the fact that apparently they are not living up to those agreements, do I take it that Canada is the stumbling block to having the commission ask for a meeting of the Geneva conference?

subtopic: PROPOSED DISCUSSIONS RESPECTING
subsubtopic: MEETING OF 14 POWER CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have already indicated on another occasion in this house that if a general conference of the 14 nations were held, Canada would participate.

subtopic: PROPOSED DISCUSSIONS RESPECTING
subsubtopic: MEETING OF 14 POWER CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think the secretary of state answered part of my question. Have Poland and India indicated that they would agree to sponsor this kind of meeting?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a question of privilege, albeit a very short one. Like the Prime Minister, I should like the record to be kept straight. The Minister of Labour said a moment ago that I misquoted him, and I did in part. I used the words "very soon" when I should have said just "soon". But he also misquoted himself, so perhaps what he actually said should be put on the record. On April 21, 1964, as reported at page 2397 of Hansard for that day, he said with respect to the labour code:
-but we hope to get it on the order paper as quickly as possible.
Then on July 13, as reported at page 5380 of Hansard for that day, he said with respect to the labour code:
-the original statement still stands-
And he then went on to say:
The measure is being drafted, and as soon as that is completed we will get it on the order paper. 1 have not had a chance to check the situation this morning, but I think the measure ought to be on the order paper soon.
May I ask the Minister of Labour whether the measure has been drafted and whether we may now expect it to be on the order paper soon?

subtopic: LABOUR RELATIONS
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO FEDERAL LABOUR CODE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I guess my original judgment that 1 should not contradict the hon. member was correct. I think my April answer is the better answer rather than the July one. We will get the labour code on the order paper just as soon as possible, and I hope that will be soon.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. When we adjourned last evening the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona had the floor.

Mr. Chairman, never before in this house have I taken so long on a subject, and I hope I will not have to again but I believe the topic on which I have embarked is of sufficient importance that none will begrudge the time.
To put it very briefly, I started last night to outline how, due to the pressure of events and changing conditions in this country, there had been a change in the policy of the government, perhaps unbeknown to the government itself, away from the first pronouncements as to the purposes of crown corporations as enunciated by C. D. Howe, who was so responsible for starting them and who showed

much energy and dispatch in creating those corporations which were necessary to carry out many of the functions that private enterprise could not cope with, especially during wartime.
I have had the opportunity of reading what I said last night. If the committee will permit, I would like to clarify a couple of points I made which I think were not sufficiently clear last night.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. May I bring to the attention of the members of the committee that it is rather noisy in the chamber and it is difficult to follow the remarks of the hon. member who has the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I mentioned this matter only briefly last night. I asked what steps have been taken to implement the report of the special committee on research, made in 1961. Many members in this house sat on that committee. The report is there. I refer specifically to the fourth report of that committee, which reveals that there had been 20 meetings. I may say that all parties were represented on the committee. We looked very closely at the business of Eldorado Mining, Eldorado Aviation, Northern Transportation Company; and in the course of those 20 meetings we heard 11 different witnesses. That committee had full opportunity to study at least some of the workings of these crown corporations. The report was brought in about the end of June, 1961.
In case any of my friends opposite want to say "What did the Conservative government do about it?" I can only say there was no concrete action taken. I do not think there was much time. Also, the Liberal government has not done anything about that report. I do not think either government would have to apologize too much for being a little slow; we all know that government moves a little slowly. But I do feel that now is the time that recommendation should be very closely looked at and I would ask this committee to listen while I read the report that pertains to the subject that I started on last night:
Your committee examined Eldorado Aviation Limited and Northern Transportation Company Limited. In the case of Eldorado Aviation, a further study by the air transport board of an offer by Pacific Western Air Lines to purchase the aviation company resulted in your committee not pursuing a more detailed examination. With regard to Northern Transportation Company Limited, your committee heard representations from officers of Yellowknife Transportation Company and Arctic Shipping Company, and heard undenied allegations that Northern Transportation Limited took advantage of its status to obtain a preferred position in
Interim Supply
transportation in the western Arctic and Mackenzie river basin.
In view of the great importance of maintaining and increasing communication facilities in the north and the need for an orderly development of Canada's northwest, your committee recommends that an impartial and independent study be made of all present transportation facilities and future needs on the Mackenzie river system and related areas.
In concluding, your committee is of the opinion that the operations and policies of Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited and its wholly owned subsidiaries require a periodic scrutiny.
Mr. Chairman, I think that last sentence would bear repeating, and I hope that what I said last night, with the further information I am going to give the committee today, will remind the government of the report of this committee and of the necessity for this periodic and in fact constant scrutiny of the policies especially of Northern Transportation Company.
I gave last night only one instance. I would remind the committee that I said I thought this was a direct case of government policy, and in fact I want to refer again to the statement of the minister on policy with regard to a crown corporation, bearing in mind that C. D. Howe, when they were set up, denied most emphatically that any crown corporation was set up for any other purpose than to fill the void where private enterprise was unable, unwilling to or could not meet the requirements. Certainly he was able to justify the crown corporations he set up during wartime, but this was in 1946, after the war, when there were suspicions that perhaps it was not necessary to have some of these crown corporations.
What I am asking the committee to consider today is the change in government policy. Here is part of the statement of the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, who has to explain to this house the policy of Northern Transportation Company. He said in part:
In performing this function the company will, as it has done in the past, operate as a normal business corporation.
I think I am being fair when I suggest that this is the hub or the meat or the core of the minister's pronouncement on present government policy with regard to crown corporations. Since we have a crown corporation set up, and since it is performing a useful service, it should be allowed to operate as a normal business corporation.
I ask this committee to consider whether or not this government is moving away beyond the position taken by the government in 1946 as enunciated by Mr. C. D. Howe.

Interim Supply
It is no longer a question of a crown corporation performing a function where private enterprise cannot or will not operate. I hope this fact sinks through to all members of this house who have some regard for private enterprise. The last sentence in the minister's statement reads as follows:
Private enterprise is also providing service and will probably continue to do so.
It seems to me that under the circumstances both Northern Transportation and the private companies operating in the north should operate at a profit, depending on the efficiency of the transportation system. I want to make sure the government acknowledge that they now believe in a policy of a government enterprise being in competition with private enterprise, and that that is fair. I want them to acknowledge also that this is an area into which private enterprise can come. There are lots of buyers ready and willing to take over Northern Transportation Company. They must acknowledge, therefore, that they appreciate having a government owned corporation in competition with a private company in this area, and that this is now the new government policy.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, the facts illustrate that despite the statement of the minister that this company is operating as a normal private corporation, this is far from the truth. There are many built-in advantages that Northern Transportation Company has that no private corporation would have. Last night I outlined one of these in dealing with the D.E.W. line supplies. I illustrated how Northern Transportation Company was expanded to take care of that situation, and how the company ignored other private firms in the north. This company had been placed in a position of trust for the private companies and, when purporting to speak for the private carriers in the north, these civil servants, these empire builders, decided this was a great opportunity to build something of their own while ignoring the private corporations.
I mentioned last night that extra transportation facilities were required by Eldorado Mining. I said it was all right to build up the company for that purpose. In view of the minister's statement that this company operates as a normal private company, I ask what normal private company is owned by its best customer. Eldorado Mining and Refining is the parent company, and Northern Transportation Company does its hauling. What other transportation company is granted a monopoly on the biggest business

in the north? How can the minister justify that statement in this house when the two biggest customers in the north, about whom there is no risk of not being paid, namely Eldorado and the D.E.W. line, are both the exclusive property of Northern Transportation Company? In the face of these facts, how can the minister say the company operates as a normal, private company?
This is not all. Last night I mentioned how Northern Transportation Company had been able, by some means or other that I have not yet been able to fathom, to get its licence to cover both sectors in the Mackenzie and the Athabasca. Here we have a situation under which for years either Northern Transportation Company or Yellowknife had to prove the need for extra service before the board of transport commissioners if they wanted to put extra tugs or barges on the Mackenzie river. There was an incident in which Yellowknife made a mistake and put a barge into service before they secured a licence. The company was fined for this. Northern Transportation Company used a tug and a barge for a year before these facts were brought to the attention of the authorities, but nothing was said. This does not sound like operating as a normal private enterprise company. Does this sound like fair competition? This is only a small incident.
What happened in connection with the equipment on the Mackenzie and the amount of competition that Yellowknife Transportation had to face are things which I am sure must stir the conscience of every member in this house. There was a special need in the Athabasca sector, and Yellowknife Transportation does not operate there. The only customer, really, is Eldorado Mining at Uranium City. Northern Transportation had a monopoly. There was a need for extra equipment because of a sudden increase in the demand for sulphur. I believe Northern Transportation had to build 26 extra barges to take care of that situation.
I have no quarrel with that. However, Mr. Chairman, for years there was a policy on the Mackenzie sector under which private enterprise operates that before an extra tug or barge could be put into service the company had to prove the need for that service. Then a bewildering change took place. In one application the Northern Transportation Company was able to have the entire basis of licensing changed. The licence of this company covers not just the Athabasca sector but the Mackenzie sector as well. Here we have a crown corporation which has expanded

to a tremendous extent, which can prove a special need for a short time in the Athabasca sector, suddenly being allowed to transfer a large fleet to the Mackenzie sector without regard for the needs of the area. I ask the minister now how he can explain government policy on that basis and still say this company is operating as a normal, private business. What is government policy?
Certainly one should look at the impact of 26 barges being made available on the Mackenzie river for competition with the only private enterprise company operating there. As I said last night, Yellowknife Transportation is trying to build itself up, and this must be done out of profits. They have to have a pretty close look at the dollar. You cannot introduce extra barges overnight. Every piece of equipment has to be working to its maximum. Yellowknife could not possibly pretend to give the same service to the public as a company that has 20 or 30 extra tugs and barges on call at any time. Yellowknife Transportation has to plan in the fall, has to work out schedules, has to look at every inch of cargo space, at every barge and what it is doing before investing another dollar. It has to look at each barge to determine how long it is going to be working and how many dollars it will bring in over how many years. Surely the minister is not serious when he attempts to give the impression in his statement that Northern Transportation is operating as a normal private business, when it can have all those barges at its call.
Not only that, Mr. Chairman, but think of this. It has a monopoly in the Athabasca sector. It sets the rates and its parent company is the only one to which it has to answer. As a matter of fact when the president of Northern Transportation was asked why there was no reduction of rates in the Athabasca sector he said "We don't have any complaints." Of course they do not. They are hauling for Eldorado Mining and Refining. They have a guaranteed rate of business, a guaranteed amount, and everything is all cushy.
Just think of this in the light of the minister's statement. What other private enterprise company in Canada can have the major part of its income guaranteed year in and year out, and then use its surplus equipment to compete with other private enterprise?
The north is opening up very slowly. The major customer for transportation on the Mackenzie is still the federal government. There is a certain amount of private business, but Northern Transportation Company has a guarantee of the business necessary to meet
Interim Supply
its expenses, has a surplus of equipment, has a surplus of money made available by the taxpayers of Canada, and thus can offer better services because it has all these extra facilities. The minister tells us it is operating as an ordinary private concern. Mr. Chairman, if the government is willing to go along with the policy as enunciated by C. D. Howe, that these companies were not set up to compete with private enterprise, then I would think there is a heavy duty on the minister to make sure that private enterprise is given a 50-50 fighting chance.
I said before that I have no argument with the personnel of Northern Transportation.
I will say that the company has a good reputation for service in the north, and I think its personnel are doing a good job. But so is Yellowknife Transportation. What we are concerned with in this chamber is policy. Do we want the taxpayer's dollar spent on this sort of thing? The committee on research dug into this very thoroughly and said we would have to keep an eye on it.
I may say that the previous government never had this pointed out to it. As a matter of fact I think until the committee on research dug into this in 1961 most hon. members were not aware that this change had taken place; and if I may be forgiven for repeating something I said last night, it was not an announced change in government policy. This was not something initiated in this chamber, or even initiated by the government. This change came about gradually. It crept in; it was pushed here and there by the empire builders of Northern Transportation and Eldorado Mining and Refining.
I say again I have no quarrel with public servants or civil servants who are doing their jobs the best they can, but I think they should have some conscience, some sense of fair play and, above all, should have some direction from government on policy as to how far they can go. Many indications have been given to me in the past that the present minister did not comprehend what was going on in the department. I only have to mention one answer which he gave me in this house about this L.S.M. Sally, an answer which is on record in Hansard.
This is the type of ship Yellowknife Transportation tried to put in but could not because it was illegal; it was too old a ship. Northern Transportation bought one, however, and I have not yet had an answer to my later question on the order paper about it. I think, without the actual purchase price, they have spent $70,000 on it since, on a

Interim, Supply
ship that it was illegal to bring in and which had previously been turned down because it was contrary to maritime regulations.
When I asked the minister did Northern Transportation Company intend to bring that ship into service he said the maritime regulations forbade its use and therefore the company had not purchased the equipment. Now, the minister is not really to blame, because he was relying on the word of some of these top public servants that Northern Transportation had not bought that boat. You cannot blame a minister for saying no public servant would have the effrontery to spend thousands and thousands of dollars of the taxpayers' money on a boat that, three years before, the maritime commission had ruled Yellowknife Transportation could not buy because it was too old.
We have a law in Canada that a ship more than five years old cannot be brought into the country. It protects the shipbuilding industry and makes sure Canada does not become a dumping ground for old ships; but here was Northern Transportation Company, pretty sharp operators, and they saw, as Yellowknife Transportation did, that if this type of ship could be purchased it could probably perform a very useful function in the Arctic. It could pull into these Arctic islands where there are little or no wharf facilities, let down a ramp and service them.
The reason Yellowknife Transportation Company had been unable to get one but Northern Transportation Company could was that Northern Transportation was a crown corporation, and it had been able to get things done to its advantage that no private corporation could; so it went ahead and bought that boat. That boat is still sitting in Vancouver harbour after a year and a half and, without counting the purchase price, Northern Transportation has spent just about $70,000 on it.
I have a question on the order paper that has not yet been answered, as to the actual purchase price of the boat. What is Northern Transportation going to do now? Despite the extra amount of equipment it already has in the Mackenzie sector; despite the fact that it has so many idle barges, it has now announced that it is building a new ship. As a matter of fact, it did not announce it; we found out. I asked the minister and he gave me an answer to this effect on-

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it is my duty, in view of my responsibilities as Minister of Justice, to take part in this debate in order to offer some comments on words spoken in the house by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) on July 30, 1964, that is last Thursday.
In his observations, he made, against Mr. Justice Pope, who presided at an inquiry on Prairie Farm Assistance Act, some charges which constitute only allegations, as he failed to back them up with facts.
The hon. member spoke in English; therefore, as I wish to criticize quite strongly some of his remarks and as I propose to quote some of them, I shall continue my remarks in the language he used.

What I am concerned with is not so much the contents or the merits of the report as the very serious accusation of political bias levelled against Judge Pope by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek without any foundation. If we read the whole of the hon. member's speech as delivered by him on Thursday, July 30, it is clear that the only reason which could possibly have motivated his accusation is that the report, as far as he is concerned, contains views which he does not share and conclusions or findings which he finds unpleasant.
A member of the judiciary was selected to conduct this inquiry because every reasonable and fair minded member of this house knew that he would apply to that hearing the same principles of equity and justice that he would display in the courtroom. I am sure that on both sides of this house members were shocked and dismayed to hear the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek attribute the commission's findings to political bias. I intend to quote very briefly from that speech of July 30 as it appears on page 6198 of Hansard.
X contend that It was not a judicial report, that it was a political report, and X am surprised that any judge, knowing the political overtones of an inquiry of this sort, would jeopardize the independence of the judiciary by acting as a judge in this connection, if not for some reason as yet unrevealed.
Later on, as reported on the same page, the hon. member continued as follows:
X would say it is a political report for more than one reason. Maybe the members of the committee do not know this, but I am informed that the judge who presided as commissioner, not in the

capacity of judge but as commissioner, was a defeated Liberal candidate in the city of Moose Jaw.
Note the words "I am informed". In the same scandalizing vein the hon. member continued as recorded at page 6201, left hand column, at the bottom of the page:
He finally comes up with a decision in which he says it was necessary and desirable that Mr. Walker be relieved of his duties. I suggest that it w?s necessary and desirable as far as this commissioner was concerned because the commissioner was a supporter of the Liberal party and Mr. Walker was a supporter of the Tory party.
And later:
That was the only reason. There was no other reason why he should have been dismissed.
Finally-this is my final quotation, because they are not too pleasant to read-I refer to page 6202, at the bottom of the page:
One of the reasons why he cannot understand, perhaps, is because he is a defeated candidate and I am a successful one. Maybe he should follow my methods.
May I say right now that this is not a very commendable example, and whoever would follow these methods ought to be condemned for using them.
This type of allegation, made with parliamentary immunity, could only serve to undermine the high and respected place that our judiciary has commanded over the years. This respect, and this integrity of the judiciary, is an essential without which the democratic system cannot operate. It is highly significant that this respect has remained unimpaired notwithstanding the fact that a large number of our judiciary have played a prominent part in the political life of our nation prior to their appointment. In every level of the judiciary, from the magistrate's court to the Supreme Court of Canada, may be found men who have laid aside their political careers to render honourable service in the administration of justice. Not infrequently they have served as commissioners in judicial inquiries under the Inquiries Act. I suggest that any member of this honourable house who impugns the integrity of the bench and attributes political motivation or bias does a great disservice to our whole system of government.

F. Davis, respectively director and supervisor of the P.F.A.A., Regina office, were both appointed by the previous administration and

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
It is true that Judge Pope was not, in the course of that inquiry, acting in his capacity as a judge but as a commissioner. However, even at that, any remarks which are slanderous or by way of innuendo or in the nature of personal attack or censure against him are unparliamentary. Citation 152(4) of Beauchesne, fourth edition, applies. It has been quoted before in this debate, and I will read it:
All references to judges, and courts of justice and to personages of high official station of the nature of personal attack and censure have always been considered unparliamentary, and the Speakers of the British and Canadian houses have always treated them as breaches of order.
I call attention to the phrase "personages of high official station". The purpose of appointing judges as commissioners is precisely to ensure that the matters before them will be dealt with by them with objectivity and a sense of justice dictated by their judicial experience. A great number of commissions were established by the government supported by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek. Some of them were headed by judges who, while they were in practice, were supporters of the previous government. For all I know some may even have been defeated candidates. It would be preposterous of

Interim Supply
anyone, on that basis, to cast the slightest doubt on their integrity as commissioners exercising judicial appraisal of the facts. Whether acting as a commissioner or as a judge, a person in judicial office has the same responsibilities, and all those I have known have discharged them honestly and objectively.
The serious part of this accusation is that although it is true that certain specific accusations may be levelled at judges on the basis of facts relating to specific circumstances which may be proven, I think it is preposterous and unfair, just from reading a report or a judgment and because it does not please the reader or goes against the grain, to conclude that the differences of opinion between the reader and the judge or commissioner have been dictated by political bias on part of the latter. If one were to accept the type of accusations formulated with great lack of responsibility by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek, one would of necessity have to lose confidence in a great part of the whole judiciary.
As a lawyer who has practised before all the courts of my province, before the exchequer court and Supreme Court of Canada and before a great number of arbitration and other boards, and as a lawyer always known to have been and to be strongly Liberal, I must give fullest credit to all the judges before whom I have appeared, either when holding court or acting as commissioners, for the fact that never have I been treated less fairly by one who had in the past professed a Conservative allegiance than by others who had, before being elevated to the bench, professed a Liberal allegiance.
One may, of course, differ with the conclusions reached. This happens in all judicial cases, because there is always one party who loses. It also happens in all cases before a board where there are two or more parties in contestation one with another. And, of course, it also happens in other types of inquiries or investigations which give rise to wider sorts of conclusions. But it surely does not mean that because the conclusion is unpleasant the judge has been either biased or unfair in making up his mind and in rendering his decision. I think it is not only improper but unfair and detrimental, both to personal reputation and to the ends of justice, for one to criticize a judge or a commissioner and to impute scandalous motives- because that is what they are-to his findings for the only reason that one's reading of the

evidence leads one to a different conclusion from that reached by the judge.
I thought, Mr. Chairman-these will be my last words-that it was my duty in my present capacity, as one whose function it is in many cases to make recommendations for the appointment of judges, to uphold and fight for the recognition of the integrity of our judiciary and to say that unless clear, positive and very serious facts are proven one must always assume-and fortunately this is the case in our great country-that the conclusions reached by a judge, either sitting on the bench or on a commission, have been dictated by the fairest and most equitable of motives.

I call to witness the member of parliament for Assiniboia who used to sit in the chamber and who now holds a high position in the Liberal party. His name is Mr. Hazen Argue. All the time he was sitting here as a C.C.F. member he always talked about the political machine of P.F.A.A. It was known in the western provinces as the Jimmy Gardiner machine. We looked into P.F.A.A., and one of the reasons why thousands and thousands of Liberals supported the Conservatives in 1958, 1962, 1963-and will again next year, or whenever we have an election-was that we ran the P.F.A.A. as honestly as any government could do it.

The reason why Mr. Riddell was appointed to that job was because I knew him for many years and knew that his reputation all over the west was one founded on honesty and integrity.

Mr. Chairman, this whole matter is not a matter of pride for any person who is an hon. member of the House of Commons. This investigation has taken place, and I want to say I was distressed during the investigation because those reporting it to the press were only concerned with one thing-what sort of scandal could they put on the front page in order to get members of parliament, like the hon. member for Medicine Hat, to stir up this awful mess, to talk in a deep sepulchral tone as if he were in a pulpit, holding himself up as "holier than thou," even though he knows that throughout western Canada today the P.F.A.A. administration has more respect from farmers than at any time in its history.
I want to put this question to my hon. friends across the way. When that investigation, directed by the minister, was called for, it was before an election. Tell me the time that the Liberal government has ever called an investigation just before an election? They would have shied away from that because they would know how many votes could be lost. We agreed, and the evidence before the Pope commission is clear, that the proper way to win the support of the public for our administration was to carry out the laws of the land honestly and efficiently. That is the reason why those six members of parliament agreed to that investigation. I can understand the point of criticizing an hon. member who might have a bad record in investigating, or in bulldozing people around and assuming they are liars before they are proven so. But all the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek argued to me was, "I don't want person X in my seat." He said, "Bring in director Riddell, but don't bring in that so and

so." Those were the words he used, only he spoke them differently. That was the only difference.
If I am guilty of anything I am guilty of leaning over on the side of my administration to make certain P.F.A.A. was carried out honestly. That is why the investigation went forward right before an election. After some delay the question came up of who would be the person who would do the reinspection in this area. I said, and these were my last instructions on it as minister, that the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek, the director and my executive assistant would meet as a group of three and whatever the three of them agreed to do, that would be my decision. The three of them did agree on a way of handling it.
Just pay it-that was the only agreement.

The voice of unctuous righteousness raises itself in the chamber again. Those three men agreed on what their action was going to be. I could go along and say a lot more than I have said, but I simply point out to many of the ministers on the front benches that sometimes you have to choose between carrying out the law of the land and delaying it somewhat. I am guilty of delaying that law by holding up from those farmers in that area the money that was theirs under the rule of parliament. I held it up for a period of three months, and under our custom there is no right to hold up that money except by evidence that there is something wrong.
As the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek points out, there was no evidence that there was anything wrong. There was a suspicion in the mind of the director, and I took my fate in my hands, if you like, by backing up the director.
I want to conclude with this one point. Whenever this parliament, judicial inquiries or any other form of educational device takes the side of bureaucracy's right to administer a thing efficiently, as opposed to the right of parliament to be supreme, this country is in a dangerous position; and that is the position that results from the end product of this report. That is the real problem raised by the Pope report. They decided that the officials of the government, including the minister, were more important than the law of parliament, because the law of parliament says that after these precautions have been taken the money must be paid at the end of December. We did not obey that law and I am
Interim Supply
guilty of backing up my civil servants. But that is the real issue. Does parliament want to surrender its power of rule in this country to the fifth estate? That is the issue. This Pope report came down on the side of the fifth estate and not of the third estate.

The hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle began his discourse by saying that his hon. friend from Swift Current-Maple Creek did not, in fact, deny an investigation. I should like to quote from page 22 of the evidence where it is stated:
Mr. Hamilton appeared before the commission and corroborated Mr. Riddell's evidence in this regard. He indicated the difficulty that he had experienced with Mr. McIntosh, who insisted that no investigation was necessary and that payments should be made.
Make no mistake about it; the minister at that time, the director and everyone else involved in P.F.A.A. have admitted that they had difficulty with the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek in making these reinvestigations early in the season. The reason it went past December, and past January, and up to those days just before the election was because, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle when he appeared before the commission-and I will read these words again-
He indicated the difficulty that he had experienced with Mr. McIntosh, who insisted that no investigation was necssary and that payments should be made.
Then, to deal with some of the other remarks made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, who was minister of agriculture at the time, let me turn to page 25. I shall quote a series of questions and answers taken from the evidence. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle is replying to the questions asked:
Q. There has been some evidence that, notwithstanding the fact that this had been turned over, that Mr. Riddell contacted you about-"shall I pay out the cheques or shall I not pay them." Do you have a memory on the subject?
A. Yes. I can't tell you the date. I recall the place. It was in the Drake hotel here in Regina. Mr. Riddell came to me about the problem again and said he was very concerned about these cheques going out and felt quite unhappy about it.
Q. Did you exercise any authority on the subject of-"Go ahead, pay them out" or "Don't pay them out"-or "Whatever Mr. Faibish says, you make your choice."
A. I don't think I put it that way. I think I do recall saying to Mr. Riddell that he shouldn't do anything that would go against his conscience, but I did say to him that I would take this matter up with Mr. Faibish again if it would make him feel any happier. I never did get the time to take it up with Mr. Faibish.

Q. You never did which?
A. I never did get a chance to take it up with Mr. Faibish.
That is from the transcript of the evidence which was given before this judicial commission, I presume, under oath. It does not square with what the hon. member for Qu'Appelle has just told us respecting his activities.
That is not a transcript of evidence, as the hon. member well knows. If we had the transcript of evidence here we could clear up these matters.

On a question of privilege. We are up against the same sort of thing. The hon. member for Medicine Hat takes a report that he does not understand and uses extracts from it suggesting there was opposition by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek to an investigation taking place. I say, here, as will be shown if this evidence is ever printed, and I say it again and again, that the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek at no time opposed an investigation. At no time did any member oppose an investigation. When the hon. member for Medicine Hat makes this allegation-
On a question of privilege.
I am speaking to a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
