Yes. I began my remarks
by saying I was rising on a question of privilege.
This is the type of attitude shown by the hon. member for Medicine Hat. He takes an official report from a very dubious report and brings out a statement by saying that I supported the evidence of Mr. Riddell. However, he does not go back and say what evidence Mr. Riddell had given, the evidence I am supposed to have supported. He picks out a little section out of context-a little something which he hopes will be some advantage to his mind, that lives in a sewer.
Oh, oh.

I would simply point out to hon. members on the government side that if they ever try to stir up any thoughts which are not based on the facts, they destroy them-

selves. The evidence given before this hearing has not even been published as yet. It will not be published for several months. I intend, when the evidence has been fully made available, to examine it very carefully, and if there is any form of malfeasance on the part of one of our judiciary I will be right in behind the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek, with both feet and both hands. This is too serious a matter to be kicked around like a political football.
Right now, I am only on my feet on a question of privilege to say that at no time did I give evidence that the investigation was refused by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek, or, to my knowledge, by anybody else. I say this in spite of the statement which was read just now out of context by the hon. member for Medicine Hat; and I should like to leave the matter there until we have the whole of the written transcript before us because there may be a very serious case before this house before very long and I would advise the Minister of Justice to make no changes in judicial appointments in Saskatchewan until this matter has been thoroughly cleared up.

I too rise on a question of privilege. I will be very brief. The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek said I did not have the evidence, or the transcript of the evidence, before me with respect to the questions and answers I quoted. I refer you, Mr. Chairman, to the top of page 23 of the report of this judicial inquiry where it is stated: "Part of the evidence dealing with this phase of the matter reads as follows:" Let me point out that I then quote directly from what followed after that statement, so what I placed on the record was taken word for word from the transcript of the evidence.

I want to put a few words on record in connection with the question of government policy as it relates to private enterprise versus government activities. On an earlier occasion I was about to read the latest answer I have obtained from the responsible minister on the subject of certain equipment. I asked whether Northern Transportation Company had placed any order, or had an order under consideration, for a ship designed to do the job for which their L.S.M. was purchased. In reply, I was told:
No, hut invitations have gone out for tenders on a vessel designed to operate in Arctic waters commencing during the 1965 navigation season. Propulsion machinery and other equipment from the L.S.M. previously purchased will be incorporated in the new vessel.

I mentioned previously that the minister had given assurances to Arctic Shipping and Yellowknife Transportation that Northern Transportation was not expanding its activities, that it had purchased the Hudson's Bay Company ship Banksland, and was going to do what the Hudson's Bay Company had been doing. I must say there has never been a more blatant case of the department misleading the minister in this regard. In fact it would appear that there could never have been a minister more easy to mislead. Then the company immediately started towing barges behind this ship and went into the business of hauling bulk oil and serving new areas. Now they are building a new vessel to expand further, and this will hit Arctic Shipping in 1965 and will kill off this private enterprise company.
There are a few more instances which show that Northern Transportation Company does not operate as a private enterprise company, that the competition it offers Yellowknife Transportation is very unfair. Let us take Eldorado Aviation, which is a subsidiary of Eldorado Mining and is a very efficient little air line. I have taken the opportunity of flying with them into Eldorado to look at their operations, and I have no quarrel with their efficiency and the management of that air line. If one believes in government enterprise and in a government engaging in private business, then these people know how to do business and are very efficient. But my quarrel is that if Northern Transportation Company, for example, forgets a small item which is part of a shipment and has to pick up personnel and transport them from one place to another in the north, it sends a request to Eldorado Aviation, and they will pick up the parcels, deliver the personnel, and so on. The minister gave an answer to the house some time ago to the effect that the government pays Northern Transportation their cost figure. If Yellowknife Transportation is put in the same situation then it goes to Pacific Western Airlines, which company, either by means of a charter flight or a regular scheduled flight, carries the personnel or the baggage and charges the rates laid down by the air transport board, rates which they must charge. And not only that, the aeroplanes of Eldorado are on call constantly, and I am sure that many of these items are never even mentioned in the account. How can the minister tell us that Northern Transportation Company is operating like an ordinary private concern?
The members of this committee may remember that I asked a question about Es-
Interim Supply
kimo houses and a tender which went out for a total of 104 Eskimo houses, although I think the initial contract was for 50. The tender called for delivery of these houses at Waterways, Alberta. Waterways, Alberta is an intermediate point. These houses will be built in Edmonton and used in the Arctic. It is common sense that the tender should call for delivery at Edmonton or in the Arctic, but it was specifically for delivery at Waterways. That is a simple example of the machinations of Northern Transportation Company. Waterways is the end of the rail line, so these houses would then have to go by barge, and only Northern Transportation operates in the Athabasca sector. If these houses are sent to Waterways, then automatically Northern Transportation will be the carrier. Had they been delivered at Hay River, at which point both companies operate, then the policy of the government would be divided 50-50. But to get around that Northern Transportation puts a plug in the right place through an adviser to the minister, and out go the tenders for delivery at Waterways.
I do not want to bore the committee with more and more examples, but I hope the members here are interested in private enterprise. The previous government only started to become aware of this problem and did not have much time to do anything about it; and for that matter I do not think this government has had much time either. But it has to do something now because this ship is being built in Vancouver. I hope the government will say right now that enough is more than enough. The minister cannot possibly stand on the statement of government policy he has enunciated. He must admit that the government is in competition with private enterprise, can use any means at its disposal and does not even have to be fair. It can take advantage of every stratagem, every benefit of its position and every sneaky way of doing business. I think the minister owes it to this committee to stand up now and enunciate government policy which will encompass the facts I have placed before hon. members, or else he should assure the committee that new directives have gone out or are going out immediately to curb this octopus, Northern Transportation Company, so as to attempt to bring their methods of doing business down to the sort of level which will make it possible for private enterprise to compete-if it is necessary for private enterprise to compete with the government.
Lastly, I would remind the minister that there was a report submitted by a committee

Interim Supply
of this house on this matter after holding 20 meetings, but nothing has been done about the report. So it is not just I who am complaining; a committee of the house has made a strong recommendation in this regard. I hope the minister will bear this in mind in his reply.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to take part in this debate on interim supply I do not apologize for taking the time of the house, in view of the fact that we in the official opposition have not had an opportunity to investigate the expenditures of this government in a discussion of its estimates. May I put on record the situation as it exists so far this session. Some 15 departments have been called and two have been completed, agriculture and post office. The estimates of the Department of External Affairs have been referred to the standing committee on external affairs after one day's debate in the committee of the whole house. Public works has been before the committee for one day; 11 other departments have been available for consideration since the supply motions of April 21, May 5 and May 26, and six more departments will be called after two more supply motions. Departments called and ready are citizenship and immigration, labour, northern affairs and national resources, industry, transport, fisheries, forestry, mines and technical surveys, secretary of state, national health and welfare and national defence. So that in this session only eight days so far have been devoted to main estimates, which is only one third to one half the time normally given to main estimates by the 110th day of the session. We are now confronted with $700 million of expenditure and are being criticized for taking the time of the house.
I should also say that in five previous sessions, going back to 1955, 1956, 1959, 1960 and 1961, this house made great use of the estimates committee. This committee always had referred to it certain departmental expenditures to investigate and examine. But what has this government done? The estimates committee was set up one year ago. Which departments have been referred to it? Has the committee met? Is it organized? The answer to all those questions is no. Why did this government not call the estimates committee together and make use of it? Why did it not put before that committee some of its expenditures? That has not been done. This is therefore the only opportunity, under interim supply, that the members of this

house have had to examine the expenditures of the government.
I should like to read what the present Prime Minister had to say in this regard when he was leader of the opposition. This is what he said in December of 1962 as reported at page 2834 of Hansard of that year:
It is a traditional and fundamental right of parliament to vote taxes before they are collected and to approve expenditures before they are made. When these rights are ignored, when they are violated, parliament itself is being violated and we are taking a step toward its destruction.
Those are the words of the present Prime Minister, yet during this debate on interim supply 230 questions have been asked by members of the opposition without one of those questions being answered to date. Yet we are being criticized for holding up this session.
The purpose of my remarks at this time is to draw attention to the Department of Industry. I am sorry the minister of that department is not in his seat at the present time.
In opening the discussion in respect of this particular department, which I am sure other hon. members of the opposition will refer to, I should like to refer to three headings. First, the establishment of the Department of Industry; second, what was our position when this department was established and, third, what has this department done since it was established? Under the third category I should like to deal with two subjects, the situation in connection with the importation of auto parts, and the matter of depressed or designated areas.
Let us first consider the new Department of Industry that was set up. This being a new department I wonder why the government did not bring these estimates before the house as the first set of estimates to be considered. The only opportunity we have had to receive any information in respect of the estimates of this department occurred on March 31, when the minister gave a short resume in introducing this department and asked the members of this house to approve the expenditure of $665,000 for the year 1963-64. In looking at the blue book of estimates I find in the year 1963-64 that the department spent not $665,000, but $14,892,000. This is the type of thing we should like to ask questions about and receive answers. I am sure we would like to ask many questions about this new department the minister has launched. That is the purpose of elected members in the opposition, and we have not had an opportunity of doing this in respect of this new department.

What was our position when this department was set up? We as the official opposition took a definite stand during the introduction or establishment of this new department in sympathy with the demand of industry. We took the position stated by the former minister of trade and commerce, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, and I will quote his remarks as they appear in Hansard of June 28, 1963 at page 1699:
This is a mistake-
He was referring to the setting up of a separate department:
-in that a very strong department, trade and commerce-which could be called industry and commerce-
This could be done simply by changing the name:
-is being weakened by this proposal.
He went on to state:
The Minister of Finance, when he was unaware Of parliamentary procedure, sold this idea to the Liberal party, used it during the election campaign and encouraged people to think that this motion could be put into operation almost overnight.
He then continued as follows:
I am suggesting that this is hasty, ill conceived legislation proposing a new department to fulfil a function which is already being carried out by the Department of Trade and Commerce.
We said at that time, as the minister has outlined, that this function was being fulfilled. We were in accord with the minister's suggestion. I admit as a member of the party which formed the last government that we set up the new Department of Forestry. What was said when we set up that new department by the then minister of justice-and I refer to Mr. Chevrier? He spoke in this house at that time and stated as reported at page 5490 of Hansard of June 28, 1960:
May I say to the Prime Minister that it appears to me that the number of ministers is already too high. In that connection a redistribution of functions and responsibilities between these departments would be highly desirable-
He said there were too many cabinet ministers. What do we find today when we look at the record of the Liberal government? We find the government has increased the cabinet from 22 ministers to 26, an increase of four. The number of parliamentary secretaries has remained constant at 16. They criticized us for establishing one new department and suggested there were too many cabinet ministers. Immediately they formed the government they increased the cabinet by four ministers.
When this new department was organized we suggested the government was empire
Interim Supply
building and that it would lead to confusion, duplicating and overlapping. This statement has pretty well been proved. I realize the Canadian Manufacturers' Association made representations to the government of the day, and probably before that, asking that some recognition be given to a department of industry, but it did not think while making that request that such a department would cost the taxpayers something in the neighbourhood of $24 million per year to operate.
I should like to quote what the general manager of that organization, Mr. J. C. White-law, Q.C., had to say:
At the same time, the association has made it clear that it does not advocate the creation of yet another ministry and department, believing that the appropriate ends could be accomplished by reorganization and de-emphasis of existing facilities.
The government went ahead and established this great empire, the Department of Industry.
At the time it was being set up what were we told? What did the press report? The Manitoba premier, Duff Roblin stated, as reported in the Winnipeg Tribune of October 19, 1963:
Manitoba government officials fear confusion and duplication will follow the giant sized federal Department of Industry recently created in Ottawa.
Feasibility studies, industrial surveys, trade missions and personnel were regarded as 'a few' areas in which duplication would exist.
The Star-Phoenix of July 12 said this:
This Department of Industry strikes us as national government paternalism on a grand scale.
In an article in the Winnipeg Tribune headlined "High-priced help" we read the following:
The federal government is beating the bushes for platoons of high priced help to staff its new Department of Industry...
Apparently the misgivings expressed by Premier Roblin and other provincial leaders have not slowed Ottawa officialdom to any perceptible extent. Federal authorities are pushing ahead in their determination to make the new industry department "fully operational" by next April 1.
We are now into August, and I do not think it is fully operational yet. The article continues:
The trouble is that Ottawa's efforts in the field of industrial development will duplicate the work being done by Manitoba and other provinces in this field. Industrial development is one of those areas in which there is divided jurisdiction between federal and provincial authorities. Unless there is co-operation, there can be waste, duplication and even working at cross purposes.
Those were some of the comments made at the time this department was set up. When we are considering the question of duplica-

Interim Supply
that was introduced by the present government. I spoke in this house on its introduction on October 3 last and again on October 16. I tried my best to bring to the attention of the Minister of Industry the folly and impracticability, as well as the unfairness of this legislation as it applies to designated or depressed areas, particularly in concentrated areas of manufacturing. He insisted that this legislation be allowed to continue. I have asked him on numerous occasions if he would change the criteria by which these areas are designated, but up to this moment no change has been made.
In the meantime, the surrounding cities of this great industrial area of Brantford-Galt, Kitchener and Guelph-continue to suffer under this discriminatory type of legislation. This is what happens in practice. An industry is looking for a new site, so it goes to the city of Galt, Guelph or Kitchener-I am confining my remarks to the area in which I live-and tells the industrial commissioner they are interested in a piece of land on which to build a factory. The commissioner takes them around and shows the industrial basin and all the facilities that go with it. He has offered them what they want, but invariably they go on to say, "We like what you have but we won't make up our mind until we go over to Brantford to see what they have because we understand there are worth-while incentives if we locate in that area."
I should like to put on the record a letter written by the mayor of Galt. This letter was sent to my good friend, and I know the friend of all members in this house, the late Gordon Chaplin. I am reading this letter with the consent of the mayor of Galt, having had it sent to me by the late Gordon Chaplin. It concerns a particular electronics control company which is presently situated in the city of Galt. They are contemplating moving a few miles over to Brantford to take advantage of the incentive offered by this designated area plan.
This is what he says:
This company proposes to reincorporate as a new company; to construct a new building on their lands in Brantford; and to purchase new manufacturing equipment. Orders presently held by this company will be turned over to the successor company for completion. In this manner this company or its successor intends to qualify as a new business. I understand that your department is aware of the procedure to be used, and has in fact given tentative approval to such a move. The company awaits only your formal certification to proceed with its plans.
(Mr. Hales.]
This is written to the Minister of Industry.
Inasmuch as the city of Brantford is just 15 miles from the city of Galt, and the designated area boundary but five miles from our boundary, one of the following three results is likely If this certification is forthcoming;
(a)	If after this company relocates, present employees choose to commute between Galt and Brantford, then the move does not alleviate Brantford unemployment, but in fact makes a dormitory of the city of Galt.
(b)	If the present employees choose to move to the new location, then Brantford will have gained an industry, but will not have improved its employment opportunities.
(c)	If the present employees choose not to commute between Brantford and Galt, then 24 persons in Galt will be unemployed.
While it is not my wish to jeopardize any legitimate and deserved benefits accruing to the Company, I must protest most vigorously any action by the Department of Industry which results in the loss of tax revenue to this community and in the loss of employment opportunities to our citizens.
I would like hon. members to take particular notice of the next paragraph:
Mr. Minister, we do not ask that the city of Galt be classified as a designated area; nor do we ask that the city of Brantford be removed from the designated area list; we simply ask that your department stop pursuing policies which make it attractive for existing industry to move from this community to any other. We are particularly resentful that public funds, to which we contribute, are the sole reason for that attraction.
The citizens of Galt and I shall most anxiously await your comments...
You can see, Mr. Chairman, what a situation this creates in an industrial area. With reference to the city of Brantford I would like to quote a few observations from the press. Here is one dated July 27, but I cannot say which paper it was in:
Brantford (CP)-Anchor Coupling Canada Ltd., a subsidiary of Anchor Coupling Co. Inc. of Liberty-ville, 111., announced Friday it will build a $250,000 plant and office here for manufacturing and selling hydraulic hose assemblies and fittings.
Brantford industrial commissioner Gordon Adams said the plant will be the first phase of a major development by the company.
Here is another:
Brantford factory plans $700,000 addition. Does it get the big Ottawa concession too? Not that Guelph and other neighbouring cities should be petty. We should rejoice. Maybe this is one step nearer the time when the "distressed area" will be removed from the backs of we taxpayers.

I thank hon. members opposite tor bearing with me. I know it is always hard to listen to those things that hurt, but I wish to say that this is the most unfair and discriminatory piece of legislation I have ever seen. One would think that it would help these particular areas and reduce unemployment in them, but it has been in operation almost a year find there is no great sign of less unemployment. There is more employment, but why should there not be after the great boost which the Conservative government gave to the Canadian economy? I have only to remind the committee of the national productivity council we established immediately after we took office, the money we put into the winter works program, the aid to the maritime provinces of $25 million a year, now increased to $35 million, the provincial grants for the vocational and training school program, the great sales of wheat we instituted, the devaluation of the Canadian dollar, the great crusade of trade and commerce to get out and sell and increase our exports, loans to farmers, hospital grants and all those other things we instituted to get the economy rolling.
Again, dealing with the designated areas, seven of them were provided for in Nova Scotia and in those seven areas there are now 209 more people unemployed than there were before the designated area legislation was put into effect in that province. It is true that there are cities which show increases. Windsor, as I say, showed a great increase due to the Bladen report, and in Ontario the city of Brantford shows 289 fewer people seeking employment as of June 1 this year compared with June 1 last year.
I do not expect the minister will reply on interim supply but when his estimates come up for consideration we will be looking forward to a complete analysis and answers in regard to this department.

Mr. Chairman, I hope I will please my supporters on the opposite side of the chamber when I have completed my remarks, and that during the course of them I will not say anything to hurt them too much, although the Minister of Industry may not agree with a few of the things I shall say. However that is politics.
The hon. member for Wellington South gave the proportion of time allotted to interim supply and the estimates which must be carefully scrutinized by the official opposition and the opposition generally, and I believe it
Interim Supply
has been shown that the official opposition is the watchdog of the treasury. Both the hon. member for Wellington South and the hon. member for Perth, who spoke the other day, pointed out that the time which has been spent on estimates to date has been much less than in other sessions.
If he were here perhaps the hon. member for Port Arthur might interpret my remarks as being on a constituency basis, because he thinks a member must not think of his constituency first. I do not agree with him in that, and the remarks I shall make will have an Atlantic flavour. First I would like to refer to an editorial which appeared in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald on June 22 this year. This was about the time there was quite a furore in the Halifax area, and indeed in Cumberland county, regarding the matter of aircraft repairs, when Fairey Aviation came into the picture.
The editorial welcomed the decision of the Minister of Industry to review the Fairey Aviation case. The editorial goes on to point out that the Minister of Industry is also Minister of Defence Production, which department is responsible for contracts for the repair of aircraft.

The freshman member will perhaps bear with me for just a moment. Having been here since 1957,1 am quite aware of what these departments contain. It is D.D.P., I think. The editorial goes on to say:
Prime Minister Pearson, in the midst of the campaign, said that his party, if elected, would establish "a federal agency for the development of economically backward areas," which was duly established under industry minister Drury, who was also made responsible for the old department of defence production.
Then it continues:
The prime minister added that there would be "direct government intervention to establish industries in hard-up areas."

He said federal tax incentives to industries locating in areas of heavy unemployment are not going to bring industry to Nova Scotia.
"Federal tax availability of such incentives in an area of heavy unemployment in central Canada may attract an industry we could otherwise have brought to some part of Nova Scotia".
These incentives are of no use because, as the premier pointed out, they are available to other parts of Canada, which means that

industries which might otherwise go to the Atlantic provinces could be lost to them. More than these tax incentives are needed.
Much has been said about the area development agency which is part of the new Department of Industry and a number of questions have been asked about it. Since we do not have the estimates before us we are obliged to get the information from the government in some way. Questions were asked as to the officials appointed to this agency.
I grant that the minister did have one meeting downstairs in this building attended by his officials. As I understand it, there are two officials to look after the Atlantic area. Apparently they have been going around the area. We do not know what they have done, and this is a question I should like the minister to answer when his estimates come up for consideration. What have they done, and where have they been? Is it expected that these officials will remain here in Ottawa or will they live in the area they are serving?
Much has been said too about the Atlantic development board. I remember the time when the legislation to set up the board was before this house. I asked the then secretary of state, now Minister of Transport, who was in charge of the measure just what difference there would be between the scope of the area development agency and the Atlantic development board. He said the board would look after such things as transportation and essential services in the maritimes and that the area development agency would be used to attract particular industries to the area. I am still a little perturbed about this arrangement. What is the connection in Nova Scotia, for example, between the Atlantic development board and Industrial Estates, the crown company set up by the Nova Scotia government? Suggestions have been made latterly that the Atlantic development board should allocate certain sums to Industrial Estates to assist in bringing in new industries. How will the area development agency fit in with this arrangement? This is a question which I hope the minister will answer at a later date.
I put questions to the Minister of Finance, and it was suggested that two industries have announced their intention to locate in my own area, which is a designated area. I realize these matters must be kept more or less secret until plans are final, but I do hope something is being done by this new department to ensure that these two industries, or whatever the number may be, will establish themselves there. We have heard nothing

since those questions were asked, and that was several months ago, so I wonder what the situation is today.
There have been suggestions that the new department can do a lot for these designated areas. I repeat that we are entitled to know what is being done. Time is passing and we have been told nothing definite as yet. The Minister of Industry is of course also Minister of Defence Production. If we go back a few years we can think of one instance where industry was encouraged in the Atlantic area. It concerns the perfection of varia-able depth sonar, which is reputed to be one of the best antisubmarine devices in the world today. In that case, the electronic equipment was manufactured by Cossor Limited in Dartmouth and the "fish", the outside part, was made by Trenton Industries in my constituency. This is an example of the cooperation which was stimulated by the former government. The other matter is, of course, the question of shipbuilding which is of such great importance to the Atlantic area. I am not discussing the defence estimates now, because I have an opportunity to speak during that debate. But the minister of defence and the government did, of course, curtail the general purpose frigate program. Nothing has been brought forward in replacement.
I am not going to go into that, but I was interested to find out what was being done as far as aircraft contracts are concerned. I asked two questions of the minister in this regard. First of all I asked the amount of contracts awarded by the aircraft branch of the Department of Defence Production from January 1, 1964 to May 31, 1964. I do not want to impute motives, but I should like an answer to this question. The former minister of industry and defence production left the government service and then returned as deputy minister of industry and defence production, and was deputy minister at the time I asked this question. He has now gone again from the government service and I understand is with the aircraft industry. The answer to this question was $99,233,187. The second question I asked was in connection with the amount of shipbuilding contracts allocated for the same period and the answer to this question was $3,470,982.71. So you see, Mr. Chairman, there is quite a difference between the two figures.
The minister may say that a number of ships have been mothballed, so the number of ships available for refits was smaller. The

reason I bring this question forward is that shipyards, especially in the Atlantic region in places like Halifax and Saint John, mean much to those areas, and their economies are affected a great deal in this way. I should like an explanation as to the difference between the $99 million and the $3 million.
We have been speaking about our Nova Scotian Minister of Labour and last week the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria asked whether our minister was holding out well on treasury board, and was able to get matters across to the other ministers. I think the evidence speaks for itself. There are the cut-backs, the Point Edward naval base situation, mothballing of ships, and so on. I am afraid that the minister has not the hold which he should have. I realize that he has to talk to the Minister of Industry and the Minister of National Defence, neither of whom is from the Atlantic area, and there is of course the Minister of Finance. I do not know whether the minister is pounding on the desk, as the hon. member for Cape Breton put it, as he should.
The hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) asked a question of the Minister of Defence Production last week, as reported at page 6002 of Hansard. He asked:
May I ask the minister whether, following his meeting with the members of the Prince Edward Island government, he is now in a position to give assurance of further aircraft repair and refit work for the Enamel and Heating plant in Charlottetown.
The minister replied:
I had a long discussion with the representatives of the government of Prince Edward Island, and I think during the course of it I persuaded them that the suggestion just made by the hon. member was quite impractical.
During the period the last government were in power this sub-plant was set up in Prince Edward Island. It has meant much to the economy of that area. Now these cut-backs have taken place and the minister has persuaded the representatives from Prince Edward Island that this suggestion of the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) was impracticable. The minister does not come from my province so I will not say too much in this regard, except that it seems to me his approach is one of a businessman, not a politician or a man who realizes that people must work to live. As I say, this has meant a lot to the economy of this area. If I may say so a lot of the minister's Westmountain approach does not go over in the Atlantic area. It may go over in other areas but we in the Atlantic areas do not accept it.

I should just like to refer to an article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal for July 14 headed: "Half of all contracts: Defence pie cut favours Montreal". Many people in the Atlantic area have seen this article by the Canadian Press and they are looking into it. Former Conservative cabinet minister George Nowlan said Monday the government's proposed new Department of Industry will be as cumbersome and confusing as an Irishman's clock.
Such a clock, he told the Commons, works this way: when the clock strikes nine o'clock and the hands read 7.30, then the Irishman knows it's 11.30.
I say that the government's clock has struck nine, the hands read 7.30 and the people, especially those in the Atlantic area, know it is 11.30.
In conclusion, and following the remarks I made in February of this year, may I say that the Department of Industry has been set up, the area development agency has been set up, so let's get moving. I said at that time that I hoped the minister would not allow his officials to sit on their fannies, and I again repeat that word. We want some answers, not tomorrow but today, and I hope the minister will provide them and take a common, ordinary, down-to-earth approach to industry as well as to defence production.

Earlier in his remarks he accused me of being a businessman, taking a practical approach and lacking in the qualities of a politician, qualities which I suppose he attributes to himself but denies to me. The hon. member asked one specific question during the time I was here and that was this. He asked the Minister of Defence Produc-

tion to explain the disparity between the aircraft contract orders placed during the three month period he mentioned from January to March of this year compared with the very much smaller figure for shipbuilding contracts placed during the same period. The simple answer to this is that the Department of Defence Production is merely the contracting agent on behalf of the Department of National Defence to procure the items of equipment and services which that department requires.
During the period prior to January 1, 1964, the Department of National Defence had in consequence of its plans, formulated the needs and justifications for the amounts of aircraft and aircraft components contracted for during the period under question, whereas during the preceding period there had not been an equivalent quantity of shipbuilding needed.
I might say this has nothing to do with the personality of the individual whom the hon. member incorrectly described as the deputy minister of defence production. The individual to whom reference was made, since his resignation from government service, did not return to it in the capacity of deputy minister of defence production. He was the deputy minister of industry, another government department, indeed. While the hon. member says he does not want to impute motives I can only conclude that his reason for raising the question at all was to do just that, and to cast doubt on the bona fides of a public servant who came back to the public service at a considerable sacrifice to himself to do a job on behalf of the people of Canada which was required to be done. The fact that he was associated with the aircraft industry before he came back into the Department of Industry, and has gone back to it again, has no connection whatsoever with the operations of the Department of Defence Production in respect of placing contracts for aircraft, aircraft components and aircraft repairs required by the Department of Defence Production. I should like to make that fact quite clear.
In respect of the hon. member's specific question about the disparity between aircraft and shipbuilding contracts I should point out that figures of contracts placed during a limited period may be very misleading indeed, and I am sure if the hon. member looks at the record of production of shipyards in Canada during 1963 and 1964, he will find that their level of output in terms of past performance has been relatively higher than has been the total output by the aircraft in-

dustry in relation to its past performance. There has been a decline in the total output of the aircraft industry in Canada greater than the decline, if indeed there is a decline at all, in the output of the shipbuilding industry. Because of the competitive system under which we operate this has fallen in different measure on different aircraft firms and different shipyards, but in fact the shipbuilding industry as a whole during 1963 and 1964 has enjoyed a higher continued level of activity than has the aircraft industry in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I am delighted to be able to take part in this debate and intend to deal with some particular problems concerning the Department of Industry. As an individual representing a part of southwestern Ontario that is heavily industrialized I can say the entire area was indeed interested in the establishment and actions of this new department. We understand this is a new department and that it will take time to level out and become proficient in the activities it proposes to carry out. However, Mr. Chairman, since we have not had an opportunity by way of discussing the estimates to delve into the actions of this department we must take advantage of means such as this to obtain the information we require. It is true there is an opportunity on orders of the day to ask various questions of ministers, but considering the magnitude of this department, this is a very poor method of obtaining the answers we require.
Mr. Chairman, in my area in the past few months there has been some increase in the activity of industry. As a matter of fact there have been new additions to factories constructed, and a tremendous amount of money has been spent in this regard. Let me assure you that the minister is not able to stand in his place and take the credit for this expansion, because it is due to two or three factors with which he is not connected. One factor had relation to the implementation of the Bladen recommendations, when concessions were made in respect of duty on automobile parts. The other factor related to the 92-cent dollar inaugurated under the former government, which put industry in my particular area in a better competitive position with United States industry, with which it is in direct competition.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to give some credit to the minister in this regard. He did send some officials of his new department to this particular area. These men were very 20220-404
Interim Supply
competent speakers and outlined in some detail the activities of the department and their hopes of accomplishment. They did in fact make reference to the business world and gave some idea of the scope of the department and how it might be used to further their interests. I must compliment the minister in this regard. I think this was a sensible and basic step for this newly organized department to take.
These men did engage in one other activity. They contacted various industrial commissioners in the area and held meetings to ascertain the problems which existed, in an attempt to decide how best they could be solved. These men did in fact entice some new industry to the area and persuaded existing industry to expand, and did so under extreme handicap. Their efforts should be highly commended.
We in southwestern Ontario are still troubled by one of the major problems that is stifling industry, and I should like to bring this situation to the attention of the minister because I am sure he in his capacity has some knowledge of it. This problem is related to the old bugaboo of unequal freight rates in respect of moving freight east and west. Southwestern Ontario is being subjected to two systems in respect of freight rates. Freight moved in an easterly direction is done so on a mile-pound rate method, whereas freight moved in a westerly direction is subject to a block rate. This system works undue hardship on industry in the area, as has been mentioned before in this house. I brought this situation to the attention of the Minister of Transport very early during this session and I am firmly convinced that absolutely nothing has been done to correct it.
This two-method system of freight rates represents one of the prime factors which cause industry to move from this area of Ontario. These industries are not in a position to compete. We can understand why the cost is twice as high to move freight from Chatham to Halifax as it is to move the freight from Montreal to Halifax, a port 600 miles east, but we cannot understand why it costs exactly the same to move freight in a westerly direction from Montreal to Winnipeg as it does to move freight from Chatham to Winnipeg. We suggest this is an inequality which works extreme hardship on industry in this area. This is one of the factors which causes hesitation on the part of industry in deciding to move in an easterly direction.

Mr. Chairman, as has been stated by previous speakers the estimates of the Department of Industry have not been before the committee as yet, so I propose to make a few general observations on this subject. The Department of Industry was proclaimed on July 24, 1963, and the minister was appointed on the following day. Up to this point, the minister has not seen fit to make any progress report to the house. One can only assume therefore that there is nothing substantial to report. The only information we have been able to secure through questioning in the house has been given in brief and evasive answers.
With all the fanfare with which this new department was brought into being, and the intimation not so many months ago that those who are in government had all the answers to the nation's problems, the citizens of this country were expecting some tangible results. Many Canadians have been disappointed, to say the least, in the meagre reports that have been forthcoming from the department. It has been in operation for about a year now, with a staff of approximately 250 and an estimated annual payroll of $4 million. It seems to me this is just a case of increased bureaucracy and an added expense to the taxpayers of the country with very little to show for it. It appears now that either the Department of Defence Production or the Department of Trade and Commerce would have been well qualified and adequately staffed to take over these responsibilities for which the government has seen fit to set up a completely new department.
Many Canadians are disturbed about this continual build-up of an already topheavy bureaucracy. However, this government has

Interim Supply
no hesitation in tacking on this extra burden. In 1945, when we had a population of 12 million we had 40,000 civil servants. Today, less than 20 years later with a population of about 19 million we are supporting 341,000 civil servants. How can this tremendous increase per capita be justified? Can Canada afford to have this trend continue? How much further can this government go with their careless handling of the country's business and this extravagant spending?
The government, following the example of the Conservative administration, has supported trade missions going abroad in search of new markets for our goods and products in this rugged world of competition. However, this same government continues to contribute to industry's overhead by way of heavy taxes which no doubt will have to be increased. Nothing perceptible has been done to help the spiralling cost of living which will be reflected in the prices of our manufactured goods by way of higher wages necessary to maintain our present standard of living. In fact, some of our industry is being placed in an almost untenable position with respect to foreign competition in our own markets. Something must be done by this government by way of reducing the tax burden if we are to make the progress that is within our capability. Such relief would help not only the designated areas, but industry right across this nation.
The Department of Industry started off with high hopes on what appeared to be a comprehensive program, but it now appears that the great optimism indicated at the beginning has lost its drive. It was said the department's primary responsibility would be to foster the efficient development of the Canadian manufacturing industry. I ask, has any effort been made in this respect? Its objectives were to create new employment opportunities, to promote research and encourage development. The only new employment so far is the staff for the Department of Industry. More specifically, the department would identify potential production opportunities in Canada and work in close co-operation with provincial departments of industry. I wonder if the minister has thought of following the example of the Ontario government by promoting a "buy Canadian" campaign.
The Department of Industry was to assist in the application of new processes and techniques and to promote research into new products. Would the minister have anything to say on these matters? Has any progress

been made in the development of better engineering design, product design and packaging? What assistance has been forthcoming in improving efficiency through work study and plant modernization, work with all agencies at various levels of federal, provincial and municipal government to provide improved industrial opportunities in designated areas?
This program for assistance to industry was made up of high-sounding phrases and, _ of course, if properly and efficiently applied could help many people in many areas. But what do we find? In the instance of benefits to industry moving into a designated area, this is made so very attractive that it creates a difficult situation for neighbouring municipalities to compete for new industry. An industry moving into an area designated by the government is given a three year holiday from income taxes, followed by a 50 per cent depreciation write-off on machinery which can be completed in two years. The third concession is a 20 per cent write-off on other equipment and new buildings to be completed over a five year period.
The Georgian bay area, in which I am particularly interested, has little chance of attracting industry because of these substantial incentives being offered to industry to locate in certain centres which already have an advantage in view of their proximity to the country's best markets. While this government continues to give prominence to matters of less importance, unemployment continues as the foremost domestic problem in our country. This is a serious situation for many Canadians, especially for the people of my area where unemployment for June increased to quite some extent over the figures for June, 1963, with no indication that circumstances will improve. I ask this government, in view of the fact that the Department of Industry has been established to help bring relief to areas with unemployment problems, what do we have to do to get some action?
On July 14 I asked the Minister of Industry this question:
Will the minister look into the possibility of having his department extend some assistance to the city of Owen Sound which now has several empty factory buildings and more unemployment than existed a year ago?

.me same ecu tonal points to the fact that Owen Sound is in the centre of a very important section of Ontario, that it does suffer from its remoteness from the great centralized industrial empire on the west end of lake Ontario, and that despite verbalized government concern expressing the desire to overcome industrial concentrations, our area has received scant attention.
In these tremendous industrial concentrations governments are forced to spend huge sums to assist municipalities to overcome the problems that their overbuilding has created. Huge highways to carry rush hour business and industrial traffic have made multimillion dollar demands on governments. Massive sewage disposal plants have had to be built. The latest development is connected with demands of overcrowded communities for greater water supplies, resulting in long and costly pipe lmes looming as the next type of subsidized works program.
The federal government has a real primary interest in bringing levelled prosperity all across the nation. Communities such as Owen Sound offer a great potential in solving the growing menace of industrial concentration but governments must take action to promote such remedial action.
During the last election campaign many outlying communities were given to understand that the bold, imaginative plans that

were to be adopted by a Liberal regime would bring new life and vigour to their communities, and that there would be plenty of work for everyone. This was another one of the decisions lost in the 60 day shuffle. The government is showing very little concern with respect to employment in the smaller centres.
On July 27 I received an answer to a question I directed to the Minister of Industry and which I put on the order paper on July 14. The question was:
Is there any way in which the federal government can assist in the stimulation of employment in the city of Owen Sound and, if so, in what way?
The reply which I received from the Secretary of State was as follows:
The federal government has introduced a number of measures of a general nature which are aimed at providing indirect assistance in stimulating employment in areas such as Owen Sound. Measures concerned with encouraging research in industry, and the establishment of the municipal loan fund are intended to stimulate employment expansion. In a more direct way, the municipal winter works incentive program and the winter housebuilding incentive program have encouraged employment expansion in Owen Sound and other parts of the country. The federal government, in co-operation with the province of Ontario, has provided extensive vocational training facilities in the city of Owen Sound. Two schools were constructed, with the federal government paying 75 per cent of shareable costs. The Owen Sound collegiate institute which was constructed at a total cost of $632,000 provides for 130 new student places. The Westhill secondary school which was constructed at a total cost of $958,000 provides for 480 new student places.
Well, Mr. Chairman, this answer refers only to measures taken by the former Conservative government, with the sole exception of the $500 bonus for winter housebuilding which, in our extreme climate, is of little benefit. I ask the government if this is to be the extent of its actions, knowing that Owen Sound has several idle industrial buildings and a large number of unemployed people registered at the national employment office? Here we have a city of approximately
20,000	people, located on a good harbour, served by two railroads and well linked with the rest of the province by good highways. Where could be found a more ideal challenge where the Department of Industry could demonstrate its usefulness? If the Department of Industry really means business, let us have some attention in our part of the province.

Mr. Chairman, a week ago today I had intended to speak after orders of the day, to make some comments follow-

ing the day long discussion of the preceding day on the Department of Labour, but the hon. member for Perth rose and drew attention to the Department of National Health and Welfare. Therefore at that time I postponed my comments. However, the remarks of the hon. member for Grey North provide a good introduction to a statement on the employment and unemployment situation, which occupied the attention of members of the committee last week.
I begin my statement with the claim that the manpower and employment policies of the government have met with an increasing measure of success. In support of that claim, may I mention only a few relevant statistics in connection with the employment record of the past year. For example, a comparison of the first quarter of 1963 with the first quarter of 1964 shows a remarkable gain of 4.8 per cent in total employment, which is almost a record. This compares with a rate of gain for the same period in the United States of 2.2 per cent; so we have in the past year made a marked impression on the employment picture in Canada. To compare the situation over a longer period, it is sufficient to indicate that our seasonally adjusted annual rate of unemployment reached a peak of 7.8 per cent in the first quarter of 1961. The comparative statistic in the United States was 6.8 per cent; we were worse off at that time than the United States. Since that peak in 1961, the annual rate of unemployment has dropped by a full 3.1 per cent to 4.7 per cent this April. The United States comparative statistic was 5.5 per cent, so we are better off today than the United States.
Hon. members ought to bear in mind when examining the employment situation that the Canadian economy has experienced a very rapid growth in the labour force in the past few years, an expansion of the order of 300,000 jobs. The economy has shown, I think, a remarkable capacity to absorb the increasing rate of labour force growth, though admittedly it has not been able fully to absorb the backlog. Nevertheless, in the past year it has made appreciable inroads into that inherited backlog of unemployment. It may help hon. members to keep the employment picture in Canada in perspective if they realize that by the last reckoning last month there were 6,760,000 Canadians gainfully employed. It is true there were at the same time 282,000 Canadians unemployed. That will, of course, continue to be the concern of the government

of Canada as it is the concern of members of the House of Commons.
In the past year, as I have stated, the economy absorbed all new entrants into the labour force and did cut into the backlog of unemployment. It is a fact that despite the existence of unemployment at the present time in Canada there are continuing and growing shortages of manpower in certain areas and in certain occupations. We have launched a number of special measures to combat unemployment and I will refer only to those which drew the attention of hon. members opposite last week and about which questions were asked. The hon. member for Yukon asked about the winter housebuilding program and I am glad to assure him that this program last year was a conspicuous success and contributed greatly to the reduction of seasonal unemployment in Canada. We believe we have achieved the two objectives of that program, namely to increase and stimulate the total demand for housing, and consequently, total employment, and also a shift construction activity from the peak summer months to the winter months when employment normally declines. We have estimated that the employment effect of this winter housebuilding program is in the amount of
200,000	jobs on site and off site. It is a matter of record that in the course of this program last year there were shortages of labour in various centres in Canada, shortages of materials and considerable activity in the off site industries. We have in that period built residential construction in the amount of $500 million. Approximately 28,000 units have applied for the special bonus, and if all structures eventually qualify approximately $14 million will be paid out in the form of incentive payments. This ought to be compared with or set off against, the drain on the unemployment insurance fund, for example, which would take place if these men, instead of being constructively employed under this program, were unemployed and in receipt of benefits. This was an experimental program. It was a new program, and we put it forward as such. It has been a success and it encourages those of us who believe that there is an increasing role for the incentive approach with the objective of increasing employment in Canada.
The older worker program was mentioned. Some hon. members, especially the hon. member for Ontario, said the effect of this program was negligible. The hon. member for Yukon asked for details about it, and I am happy to provide this information. This, too, was an
Interim Supply
experimental program and the information gathered from it, together with the results of its operation, are being examined by the Department of Labour with a view to developing a better and more effective older worker program, if possible, in future years. But at the end of April a total of 1,912 workers aged 45 and over had been placed in approved jobs or hired directly by employers. That total of almost 2,000 jobs is an important total if it represents, as I believe it does, a solution to the problems of almost 2,000 older workers who for a long period of time had failed to find effective employment on the labour market.
The municipal winter works incentive program was more effective than ever. The number of man-hours increased. The total number of projects increased. The total of our federal payments increased. This happened because we have made available 60 per cent of payroll costs in designated areas and areas of high unemployment, and because we have reduced the effective period of the program from seven and a half months to six months, thereby concentrating employment activity in the period of peak seasonal unemployment. We are however at the present time searching within the Department of Labour for methods of meeting what has been presented as a problem, namely the seasonal, or temperature, or weather variations between one part of Canada and another which affect adversely the completion of these programs in certain areas.
The hon. member asked about expenditure in the last fiscal year by way of capital assistance for vocational and technical training schools. Last year payments to the provinces under this program amounted to about $102 million. The hon. member for Ontario asked what progress was being made in connection with the separation of the national employment service from the unemployment insurance commission. The committee of senior civil servants, including the secretary of the treasury board, the chief commissioner of the unemployment insurance commission and the deputy minister of labour, are currently examining how this separation can be effectively undertaken, and this problem is well in hand.
The problem of automation has not been neglected, and I would reply to questions in that field by telling hon. members that the manpower consultative service is presently in operation, and has been for a period of three months, with a staff consisting of the director, three officers and a small supporting staff. The director and the officers have made field visits to Vancouver, Toronto, Montreal,

Interim Supply
Saint John, Moncton, Halifax and St. John's for discussions with provincial authorities and the representatives of both management and labour with regard to the application of the government's program of research incentives and mobility incentives to meet the problem of automation.
Hon. gentlemen have asked about activities in connection with regional development. I will meet directly one or two questions which have been raised by indicating to hon. members that the Atlantic development board has at its disposal a fund of $100 million for projects in the Atlantic provinces, and at the present time more than half of this total has been approved for development projects. So that this ought to have a very distinct effect in accelerating the economic development of the Atlantic provinces.
It may be useful to hon. members if I indicated the improving employment situation in the Atlantic provinces. As of last June the unemployed in the Atlantic provinces amounted to 5 per cent of the population, a relatively high regional rate but lower by 1.4 percentage points than the year preceding and reflecting a decrease in the total unemployed over that year of 7,000 and over the two-year period of 15,000. It is a fact that various parts of Canada still have a relatively high rate of unemployment; but it is also a fact that in the Atlantic provinces, among the highest regional rates there has been an appreciable improvement reflected in the percentage of unemployed, total unemployment and the growth of total employment.
We have under consideration the Gill report. The hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale has risen again to this subject which interests him so much in light of the possibility in the future of including farm workers under unemployment insurance coverage. All I can say at this time, Mr. Chairman, is that we are eager to press ahead with this particular phase of our legislative program, but as indicated by the Prime Minister this must take its place in light of the program which was announced in the speech from the throne. However it is not something which we are neglecting or of which we are unaware, and I should like to assure my hon. friend that that is the case.
I cannot refer to all the employment matters which were raised in speeches made by my hon. friends from Nova Scotia because they did cover a very wide field indeed, but because of the questions asked by the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria I

should like to indicate to him my conviction that the long term employment outlook for the island of Cape Breton is, in my judgment, a very excellent outlook indeed. It is estimated that the construction phase of the heavy water plant will provide employment for
2,000	workers, and that will indeed be of very great assistance in alleviating the unemployment problem and providing additional employment on the island of Cape Breton. There is in the interim a short term unemployment problem which has been created by the lay-offs at the Point Edward naval base and the single shifting of No. 18 colliery.
We are attempting to meet this short term problem by a decision taken by cabinet some weeks ago to accelerate our spending program on the island of Cape Breton. The area development agency has been authorized to co-ordinate their activity and at present four government departments have under consideration a list of projects which, if it is feasible, we hope will be accelerated on the island of Cape Breton to meet this short term unemployment problem which we think will be considerably eased over the longer period.
The problem of the opening of a new coal mine at the Lingan seam has interested the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria, and all I can say to him is that the Atlantic development board has been considering the whole problem of production and employment in the coal industry of Cape Breton and Nova Scotia. It is depending for the completion of its studies upon data to be provided by the Dominion Coal Company, and it is expected that that data will be provided in full some time this month. Following that, the Atlantic development board and the government will be able to consider or hope to consider a longer term policy for production and employment in the coal industry in Cape Breton.
Mr. Chairman, I have made some effort to answer some of the questions put by hon. members opposite relating to employment and employment projects, and they can be assured that they will have a full opportunity to ask further questions when the estimates of the Department of Labour are formally put forward. Before I take my seat I should like to refer to a number of questions which were asked by hon. gentlemen opposite in the field of labour relations and to reply to a number of comments which were made particularly with respect to the maritime trusteeship.

I wonder whether the minister would permit a question before he moves on to that aspect of his speech. I understood him to say that there would be approximately 2,000 people employed during the construction of the heavy water plant. Could he indicate approximately how many permanent employees there will be, once the construction phase is completed and the plant is in operation.

Mr. Chairman, total employment within the heavy water plant itself, as I recollect it, is estimated to be in the neighbourhood of 200 additional employees. There will be additional employment created also in ancillary activities, especially the additional power facilities which will be required in conjunction with the operation of this plant.

Would the minister answer a question at this time on vocational training. In referring to vocational training the amount spent last year-I think he said last year- was $102 million. How much of that was contracted for in, say, the year 1962 or up to April 1963? Would the minister have any figures with regard to that? I am trying to make a comparison between the amount spent on vocational training or buildings under the former government and this government. Does the minister have that figure?

Mr. Chairman, I would concede at once that payments made as at the end of the past fiscal year are less than the payments made in the immediately preceding fiscal year. I do not think political capital can be made one way or another about these variations in capital investment, because this really has to do with the kind of development that took place in the vocational training field.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask one more question but shall preface it with a short remark. I am not trying to make political hay out of this situation but merely point out to the minister a fact which is probably well known to him. By the end of 1962 the vocational training program in Canada in respect of school buildings and equipment was practically complete. Naturally if a school is contemplated early in 1962 payments may not be made until well into 1963. That is the point I wish to make at the present time. I ask the minister whether he can give me an answer to my question. If he is not able to do so at this time perhaps when his estimates are before us he will be

able to give me those figures. When did vocational training finally dry up? In other words, from 1963, on, how many new projects were in existence? We all know the growth was phenomenal up to the end of 1962.

I will be glad to provide
those figures in detail in respect of my estimates. I do expect there will be increased activity and payments because the province of Quebec will take advantage of this program.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few comments dealing with matters that were raised in connection with the maritime unions trusteeship. Last October the government introduced legislation in this house to provide for a trusteeship over the five maritime unions. I am glad to say that at that time the discussion in respect of that trusteeship was conducted in an almost completely nonpolitical atmosphere, and the proposal received the almost unanimous support of all members of the house. Every amendment that was proposed by any member in any part of the house was accepted by the government, so it is indeed a fact that that act now governing the trusteeship is a product of the House of Commons in a real sense.
Mr. Chairman, there has seemed to be, within recent weeks or months, a sense of frustration on the part of certain members of the house in respect of the operation of the trusteeship. It may be that some of the comments I will make will help to relieve some of the anxiety that has been expressed in respect of the operation of the trustees. You will recall that these men were appointed to their posts on October 23, 1963 and on that occasion members on all sides of the house, including the Leader of the Opposition, testified to the high quality of each of the trustees. There is no doubt that serious effort was made to obtain the best type of person to serve on the board of trustees. The house recognized the quality of these men as evidenced by the remarks recorded in Hansard of October 23, 1963. These men are the same men that received the confidence of the house less than a year ago. I should ask hon. members as they assess the contribution, as they assess how the trusteeship has operated, as they assess how this difficult and delicate task has been discharged by the trustees to bear in mind the number of real achievements that are to be credited to the board of trustees.
When these men were appointed and called to Ottawa all the S.I.U. ships were tied up. All the S.I.U. members were off these ships

Interim Supply
milling around and about the S.I.U. hall in Montreal. The trustees summoned the president of the S.I.U. to Ottawa and subsequently all the seamen returned to work and normal traffic was restored on the great lakes. We are well into the 1964 shipping season and we have witnessed a season of complete peace and harmony on the great lakes. The violence, the dynamiting and harassment to Canadian shipping in United States ports has ended and the rule of law has been observed in respect of all Canadian ships, including the ships of the Upper Lakes Shipping Company. That is something that hon. members should bear in mind in assessing the work of the trusteeship. They have brought real economic benefit to Canada in the past year.
May I just refer to the performance of the shipping industry in the shipment of wheat and flour. At July 22, 1964 we had exported 571 million bushels of wheat and flour from Canada by ship. That is a record performance. The last previous year of high exports from Canada for a shipping year was in the crop year of 1928-29 when we exported 354 million bushels. We must compare 354 million bushels for the last record year of 1928-29 with 571 million bushels as at July 22 this year.
I am sure we exceeded 600 million bushels of wheat exported by the end of July or by the present date, August 4. That is a rather significant performance. In addition we move by water approximately 70 million bushels of feed grain to eastern locations.
I merely point this out, Mr. Chairman, because this achievement would not have been possible without the contribution which the board of trustees has made in the restoration of normal shipping to the great lakes in this country.
Would the minister permit a question?
Yes.

I think this is an opportune moment to ask the minister whether the trustees at this time have expressed a willingness to appear before the standing committee on industrial affairs, and perhaps I should add, in camera if necessary?

Mr. Chairman, I will be glad to deal with this point later on.
The board of trustees has removed Mr. Banks, the former S.I.U. president, from office, and I really do not take very seriously the charges made by the Leader of the Opposition that Mr. Banks is a coddled pet of the Liberal party. A government appointed trusteeship has removed Mr. Banks from

office. Government appointed special counsel have investigated the activities of Mr. Banks. An incident took place in 1957-
We tried to get you to do it then.

An incident took place in 1957 and has resulted in a criminal conviction. Mr. Banks has been sentenced to five years in jail. That conviction is subject to appeal. A government appointed special counsel accomplished that.
He sloped off.

In addition government appointed special counsel have laid at least two additional charges against Banks. These charges will ultimately be heard in the Canadian courts. So I say to the Leader of the Opposition, with friends like that Mr. Banks hardly needs any enemies.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, would the minister permit a question at this point? Were the charges laid and the special counsel appointed as a result of the initiative of the government, or was it as a result of Judge Norris' recommendation?

It resulted from the initiative of the government, because this incident that took place in 1957 could have been the basis for criminal action to be taken by the government of which my hon. friend was a member. These facts were well known. This beating was well known when it occurred in that year. I would like hon. members opposite to explain at some time why all those years were allowed to pass without any investigation or any action by that government, in the face of facts that were publicly known at the time and were known to the government.

Mr. Chairman, I would ask the minister just one more question and I will not interrupt him again. Would the minister not admit that it was the fact finding of Judge Norris that eventually pushed the government that was then in office, of which the hon. minister is a member, and brought about the appointment of special counsel and eventually the conviction of Mr. Banks? Was that not done on the recommendation of Judge Norris?

Mr. Chairman, it is a fact that Mr. Justice Norris did suggest that special counsel be appointed, and action was taken almost immediately. But that does not in any way alter the fact that it was open

to the government of which my hon. friend was a member to take action on the facts, on the events that took place in 1957 and which were well known to the government. And nothing was done over that long period of time. I would like some day an explanation from the Leader of the Opposition for that long lapse of time.
Would the minister permit a question?

I would like to finish my remarks, and then I will answer any questions that I can. I think the board of trustees have made another contribution in changing the direction of S.I.U. propaganda. They have done some important things in this field.

Mr. Chairman, I thank the committee for allowing me to continue. I will not abuse the privilege given to me, but I just wish to refer to one or two other points. I do not regard this as a complete and comprehensive report on this subject at all. The board of trustees have attempted and have succeeded in doing something which was long needed in the maritime shipping industry, and that is to encourage the establishment of joint collective bargaining with employers in that industry. These are some of the positives that ought to be considered as hon. members assess what was bound to be a very frustrating job that we assigned to the board of trustees.
I recall very vividly that debate on second reading when I and other hon. members said this was going to be a tough job. When I brought the bill in first, the period of the trusteeship was five years because I thought it might take that long. Nine months have

elapsed and there is still a long period of time required before the complete reconstruction along democratic lines, the restoration of democratic habits and the restoration of democratic attitudes can take place in this particular union. Hon. gentlemen have talked about an arrangement or a deal between the board of trustees and Mr. Paul Hall.
We want to hear about that.
I am always glad to oblige my hon. friend from the Kootenays.
